title: Intermarket Relationships
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/0/body: The **DXY** shows the value of the US dollar against a basket of **6 major currencies**: the euro, yen, pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona and Swiss franc. The **euro** has the biggest weight, at about **58%**.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/1/body: When the DXY rises, the dollar has gotten stronger, so **EUR/USD** and **GBP/USD** usually fall and **USD/JPY** usually rises. **Gold**, which is priced in dollars, often has an **inverse** relationship with the dollar too. These are **correlations, not rules**.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/2/prompt: The DXY is up 1% today. What has EUR/USD most likely done?
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/2/explan: The euro makes up more than half of the DXY. A stronger dollar means a lower EUR/USD; the two are usually close to mirror images.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/3/prompt: This is the Dollar Index trend. What's the more sensible expectation for EUR/USD?
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/3/explan: The DXY is making higher highs and higher lows, so the dollar is strengthening. Since the euro is the biggest part of the DXY, EUR/USD usually comes under downward pressure.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/4/statem: Since the euro has the biggest weight in the DXY, the DXY and EUR/USD usually move in opposite directions.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/4/explan: A rising DXY means a strong dollar, and a rising EUR/USD means a strong euro against the dollar. So the two usually have an inverse relationship.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/5/body: If the dollar has strengthened against **every** currency, the story is probably **the dollar itself** (say, US news). If only EUR/USD has dropped and the others haven't moved, the story is probably **the euro**. The DXY helps you see which side the move is coming from.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/5/tip: Before trading dollar pairs, take a quick look at the DXY chart.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/6/senten: When the DXY rises, USD/JPY usually goes ___, and gold usually sees ___.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/6/explan: In USD/JPY the dollar is the first currency, so a strong dollar means a higher USD/JPY. Gold is priced in dollars and usually comes under pressure when the dollar is strong.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/7/prompt: Today EUR/USD, GBP/USD and AUD/USD all fell, and USD/JPY rose. What's the most likely explanation?
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/7/option: The euro weakened on its own
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/7/explan: The only thing these four pairs have in common is the dollar. When every pair moves in the dollar's favor, the main story is dollar strength, not weakness in some other currency.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l1/steps/8/pairs/: The dollar vs. a basket of 6 currencies
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/0/body: When investors feel **optimistic**, money flows into **riskier, higher-return** assets: stocks, crypto and currencies like the **Australian dollar (AUD)** and the **New Zealand dollar (NZD)**.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/1/body: When **fear** takes over (crises, wars, sharp market drops), money flows into **safe havens**: the US dollar, the **Japanese yen**, the **Swiss franc**, **gold** and government bonds. These are **common tendencies** and don't always repeat exactly.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/2/prompt: A sudden geopolitical crisis is in the headlines and stock markets are falling. Which asset is most likely to see safe-haven demand?
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/2/explan: The yen is a traditional safe haven, and demand for it usually rises when fear takes over. The other options are risky assets.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/4/body: Since AUD is a risk-loving currency and JPY is a safe haven, many traders treat **AUD/JPY** as a thermometer for market mood: when it rises, that usually goes with **risk-on**, and a sharp drop usually goes with **risk-off**.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/4/tip: Crypto often gets hurt along with stocks in risk-off shocks too.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/5/prompt: AUD/JPY dropped like this. Which market mood does this move fit best?
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/5/explan: A sharp drop in AUD/JPY means the risk-loving currency (AUD) weakened and the safe haven (JPY) strengthened. That's a common sign of a risk-off mood.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/6/statem: In a risk-off mood, currencies like AUD and NZD usually get stronger.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/6/explan: AUD and NZD are risk-loving currencies and usually strengthen in risk-on. In risk-off, money mostly flows to USD, JPY, CHF and gold.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/7/senten: In a ___ mood, money usually flows from stocks and crypto into safe ___ like the yen and gold.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/7/explan: Risk-off means fear is in charge, and investors care more about protecting their money than earning more.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/8/prompt: US stocks hit a record, Bitcoin rose and AUD/JPY went up, while the yen and gold are weak. Which statement is more accurate?
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/8/option: The mood is risk-on, but these correlations can change suddenly
The mood is risk-off; money is fleeing
The mood is risk-on and will stay that way forever
These markets have no relationship at all
lessons/fundamental-u3-l2/steps/8/explan: Every sign (stocks, crypto and AUD up, safe havens down) points to risk-on. But market mood can flip fast on a single piece of news.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/0/body: A **bond** means lending money to a government or company in exchange for a set interest payment. The **yield** is the return a buyer gets at the current price. **Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions**: when the price falls, the yield rises.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/1/prompt: US bond prices have dropped. What happened to their yields?
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/1/explan: A bond's payment is fixed. When you buy the same payment for a lower price, your percentage yield goes up. So a lower price means a higher yield.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/2/body: The **US 10-year Treasury yield** is one of the most important numbers in the market. A rising yield usually supports the **dollar** and puts pressure on **gold** (which pays no interest) and growth assets like **tech stocks and crypto**. Again: **a tendency, not a rule**.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/3/statem: Higher bond yields make holding gold, which pays nothing, relatively less attractive.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/3/explan: When safe bonds pay more, the "opportunity cost" of holding gold, which pays no interest, goes up.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/4/prompt: The US 10-year yield has been rising for weeks in a row, and gold has moved like this. Which explanation makes the most sense?
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/4/option: Holding gold now costs more in lost yield
Gold has nothing to do with rates
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/4/explan: Gold is in a downtrend, which fits rising yields: bonds have become more attractive, and the dollar usually gets stronger too. But other factors, like safe-haven demand, can break this relationship.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/5/body: Long-term bonds usually yield more than short-term ones. When the **2-year** yield rises above the **10-year**, the curve is said to be **inverted**. This has happened before many US recessions, but it's **not a sure forecast**.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/6/senten: The yield curve becomes ___ when the ___-year yield rises above the 10-year yield.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/6/explan: Normally, lending for longer demands a higher return. When short-term bonds pay more, the curve has flipped, or inverted.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/7/prompt: US CPI came in hotter than expected, and the 10-year yield jumped. Which combination of reactions is more likely?
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/7/option: Stronger dollar; weaker gold and tech stocks
The dollar and gold both surely flat
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/7/explan: Hot inflation means higher rates are expected. Yields rise, the dollar usually strengthens, and gold and growth assets come under pressure. That's the main tendency, but it can differ each time.
lessons/fundamental-u3-l3/steps/8/pairs/: A loan to a government or company with set interest
A bond's return at the current price, in percent
